For a complete copy of the records and of all the evidence given before the royal commission, appointed under the Public Inquiries Act, regarding the Hong Kong expeditionary force, together with all papers, letteis, telegrams, and other correspondence relating thereto, and a copy of the addresses of counsel in the case, other than that already tabled.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have already given the house, on two or three occasions, the reason why much of the information asked for in this motion cannot be given. The order asks for a complete copy of the record and of the evidence given before the royal commission regarding the Hong Kong expeditionary force. The record, as my hon. friends must know, includes many communications from the British government to the Canadian government and other communications that are of the most confidential character and which could not possibly be disclosed without giving to the enemy information which should not be given. The commissioner, the chief justice of Canada, has embodied in an appendix to the report those parts of the evidence which he regarded as essential and in the public interest to publish; and _ I should think the known standing of the Chief Justice of Canada, who was commissioner in that inquiry, should be sufficient reason for the acceptance of his statement that the information which is essential is included in the report.

I desire to take issue with the Prime Minister with regard to the substance of his statement. In the first place the Prime Minister indicated, in reply to an inquiry by the hon. member for
Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), that some facility would be afforded for discussing the Hong Kong report. At the same time, on every occasion on which this material has been asked for, the government has taken every means within its power to frustrate any debate on this important topic, first by withholding the evidence or such portion of it as it would be in the public interest to have tabled here, and second by resorting from time to time to an alleged rule that a certain inquiry is sub judice and therefore cannot be discussed. A further reason advanced has been that the inquiry was held in camera. That I submit is no reason at all why we should not have the evidence. All these factors combine to make it impossible for this House of Commons, denied all the evidence and all exhibits, to come to any real conclusions as to justification for the report, not of the Chief Justice of Canada but of a royal commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act.
Since when has there been a rule that this House of Commons should not criticize a report of a royal commission? The implication that is made by reference to the Chief Justice of Canada is merely a method to evade a proper discussion of this report; and I protest against it. It is not the Chief Justice of Canada who made the report; it is a royal commissioner appointed by this government. Further, if we are to have any debate on the Hong Kong report, how in the world can we arrive at any dependable conclusions; how can this House of Commons come to any conclusions at all, unless we have the evidence before us to ascertain whether the conclusions of the royal commission were justified or not?
I submit that it is within the right of this House of Commons to order that the evidence, such as is not inter-governmental-and I reserve judgment on that for the moment- should be tabled. Without that the government makes it impossible to discuss this report or to arrive at any just or dependable conclusions with respect to the accuracy or otherwise of the report of the royal commissioner. I submit that this motion, either in its present form or in some amended form, should as a matter of right be passed by this House of Commons.

Under the rules of the
house, I admit, I am bound by the Prime Minister's statement. It is about the same as that which was given in the British House of Commons on June 11 by Mr. Attlee in answer to Mr. Stokes. I should like the Prime Minister to look that over. I may say that on March 11, Mr. Eden, in the British House of Commons, gave details of the whole
Motions for Papers

story. It is no reflection on anyone in the government here, but if the information had been given to the country weeks before that, Singapore in my opinion would not have fallen. It would have been better if the men at Singapore had died with rifles in their hands so as not to have the murder of prisoners as at Hong Kong, and Singapore would have been saved. What was done at Hong Kong with our men was known to Canada, because the same thing was done to the Chinese in 1933, and it shocked the whole civilized world. While I am bound by the rules of the house on a motion of this kind, I urge upon the Prime Minister the advisability of acceding to the request that has been made. I do not wish to embarrass the government but I really think that in the future it would be far better to let the people of Canada have the whole facts. No one knows what the Japs may do next. If they come to Canada we may expect the same savagery.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: First of all, may I say to my hon. friend (Mr. Hanson) that the government has not sought in any way to frustrate a debate on the subject of the Hong Kong commission's report.
What I said was that the effect of the government's attitude was to frustrate it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I indicated that opportunity for debate would be given, and it will be given. My hon. friend requests that all the evidence be tabled. May I remind hon. members that when the subject of the inquiry into the Hong Kong expedition came before the house it was at first suggested that the investigation should be by a committee of this house. On reflection, all leaders of the different parties in the house were agreed that it would not be advisable to have the inquiry made by a committee of the house, in that among other reasons, much of the information that would be essential might, if given in public, afford information to others, the enemy in particular, which it was not desirable they should have. Much of it would necessarily be confidential, and it was decided that it would be better to have the inquiry conducted by a royal commission.
The next point that came up in considering the personnel of the commission was whether or not the inquiry would necessarily be in camera or in public, or in part one and in part the other. There again the understanding, or at any rate the feeling, was that the inquiry would necessarily have to be at least in part in camera, and that the commissioner himself should be the judge of the extent to which publicity should be given the proceedings. It

is in that connection that I referred to the office which the commissioner holds at the present time.
The commissioner was the Right Honourable the Chief Justice. The Right Honourable Chief Justice Duff was chosen for that position as commissioner because it was felt that his knowledge of procedure in matters of the kind, his judgment as to what it might or might not be in the public interest to disclose with respect to the significance of the Hong Kong inquiry, would not be questioned from any source.
If I am not mistaken, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition said from his seat in the house-if he did not say it from his seat in the house, he said it to me personally- that in his opinion no better choice could possibly be made than the chief justice to conduct the inquiry, that he had implicit regard for the integrity of the chief justice, and that no question would likely be raised with respect-
No one is attacking his integrity.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, but I am explaining the reasons why it was thought advisable to appoint a royal commission, and why the chief justice was chosen. It was the knowledge that of necessity the inquiry would have to be held in camera, if not in whole at least in part. So that to that extent at least there are the strongest of reasons why only such evidence should be produced as the chief justice himself has thought advisable. The commissioner, in addition to his report, has presented an appendix to the report which gives what he, the commissioner, says is the evidence that he regards as all that is essential to make public. This does not mean that what the commissioner has withheld is something that is withheld for any political reason. No one in the world would say that Chief Justice Duff, as commissioner, would withhold any evidence from a motive of the kind. Any evidence which the commissioner had not thought it advisable to have made public, and which is not published in his report, has been withheld undoubtedly for reasons which in his judgment are of first importance in the public interest. That reason and that reason alone is the one which actuates the government in declining to place further evidence on the table.
The Canadian end of it should not be secret.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not propose to set my judgment up against either my hon. friend's or that of the commissioner.

Motions for Papers
It would not compare very favourably.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If I had to choose between the two I should prefer to take that of the commissioner. As to there being a right to criticize the report, no one has said that this House of Commons has not that right. Any hon. member may say whatever he pleases with respect to the report and criticize it in any particular. That is his right and, may I say also, his responsibility.
My hon. friend speaks of the matter being sub judice as having been made an excuse for not having a debate on the subject. The matter is not sub judice at the present time: The report, has been laid on the table of the house and it is available for discussion. The reason for our not having had the discussion up to the present time is that matters of more immediate importance have been before the house since the time the report was laid on the table.
In conclusion, may I remind hon. members that following the procedure the government had before it the example of another inquiry which, if not of greater significance, was at least of equal significance. I refer to the inquiry made by the government of the United States into the Pearl Harbour situation. A judge of the United States court and others were appointed commissioners. The inquiry was held in camera. The commission made its report, and so far as I know no request has been made for the production of the evidence. Certainly the commissioners have thought it inadvisable that the evidence should be made public.
They took action.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What action does my hon. friend propose that we should take?
Let us have the evidence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend cannot suggest any other action but, "let us have the evidence." Where he stated that the United States commission had taken action, it was immediately after I had said that none of the evidence was placed before the country by that commission. However, this is not the time to argue the matter of the Hong Kong inquiry. For the present, all I wish to say is that the government does not feel that it is in the public interest to comply with this request, and the government will not agree to the motion.
Was a copy of the Duff report and blue book sent to the British government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: All these important matters are communicated to the British government.

Will the right hon. gentleman be good enough to look at Mr. Stokes' question in the British house on June 11, and Mr. Attlee's reply? I sent it over to him. He says that the Chief Justice of Canada wired to ask the British government to release the telegram which was sent, by Great Britain asking for this expedition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have just been handed a copy of the Parliamentary Debates of the House of Commons of Great Britain, official report, dated June 11, 1942, from which I quote:
Mr. Stokes asked the Prime Minister whether the decision to reinforce Hong Kong shortly before its fall was recommended by his military advisers; and how long it was anticipated that such reinforcements would enable Hong Kong to hold out?
Mr. Attlee: His Majesty's government have ne further statement to make on this matter at the present time.
Mr. Stokes:	Are the government likely to
receive a copy of the report by the Lord Chief Justice of Canada to the Canadian parliament on Hong Kong, and will they study it?
Mr. Attlee:	There is a later question on

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the house was in committee on the bill on Friday last I was not able, owing to arrangements I had made, to be present during the discussion. But I have read the debate since, and I find that in answer to requests that individual fishermen owning boats or gear should receive some protection from this type of measure an order in council was passed, quite independently of the scheme, under which payments on the basis of compassion are to be made to fishermen through the Department of Fisheries at the will and pleasure of the Minister of Fisheries.
I read the minister's statement in giving that information, and I gather that the order in council was not available at the time the discussion took place on Friday last, and has only since been distributed, but I am unable to arrive at a proper comprehension of the reason why this method was adopted dehors the bill itself and why it should not be made part of a comprehensive scheme of insurance even if the anticipated recipients are not paying any premium, and of what the insuperable difficulties are to including this provision in the statute itself rather than in an order in council which may be repealed at any moment at the whim and pleasure of the minister.
The objection to this method of procedure by order in council is that it is the most temporary kind of legislation. It can be wiped out by a stroke of the pen. There is no^cer-tainty about it. It has not the force of a statute inasmuch as a statute can be repealed only by parliament, while this may be repealed by council on the recommendation of the minister, and I take the ground that that is not good enough for these fishermen if they are in a position where they require protection of this kind.
Furthermore, I object to this order in council on the ground that it leaves everything to the whim of a minister, who, if he wanted to be arbitrary, could take action whereby not one dollar of compensation could
be paid to any person. The power is purely discretionary on his part. Section 2 of the order in council reads:
The minister may pay compensation to any person in the amount, not exceeding $2,000, of each diminution of value caused by war damage in any fishing boat of which he is the owner; provided that if any person is a joint owner his compensation, hereunder, shall be limited to his proportionate share of the said $2,000.
The compensation with respect to gear must not exceed $400, and in no case shall small claims less than $25 be paid. The whole thing is left to the discretion of the minister.

I am dealing with one particular thing, and may I say with great respect to the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare, that I am asking the minister for an answer to my question just why this method was adopted, and why this protection is not incorporated in the bill. Would it upset the whole balance of the scheme to include it in the bill? I have not formed an opinion, because I realize that this is a technical matter, and I presume that there have been calculations, mathematical, actuarial and what-not, in relation to the whole scheme, and that this is an intrusion on the scheme; I think it is fair to say that. It is a new element being injected at the demand of hon. members who, very properly, have made this demand. But just why is it impossible to put this in the bill and make it part of a statute instead of an order in council, which depends in large measure upon the good-will and bona fides of a minister?
If I wanted to be very critical I could say this, that in the hands of a politically-minded minister-and we have seen this sort of thing worked in days gone by in other fields of activity, not particularly in the maritime provinces, but further west, we will say-the granting of public money might be open to the very gravest abuse, open at least to charges of favouritism, open at least to pressure, open to some form of duress, especially if pay-day came around about the time of a general election. Can one imagine any instrument in the hands of an unscrupulous minister that would be better fitted to drive right into the ballot boxes the votes of the would-be recipients of this largesse, because it is to be granted on grounds of compassion; it is not a grant ex gratia, not a grant as of right.
The principle seems to be absolutely wrong, and unless there is forthcoming a satisfactory answer I do not think we can accept this.

Mr. Chairman, the provisions of the
order in council referred to by the leader of the opposition were carefully considered. Members of this committee will recali that when the insurance bill was first before it, several members representing constituencies where fishermen reside pointed out that there was no provision in the bill for state insurance of fishing boats.
It was then stated by the Minister of Finance at my suggestion that the matter of protecting fishermen against loss by war damage was under consideration; that damage to the person of a fisherman by war accident was already provided for by order in council under the War Measures Act; that the protection of the personal belongings of a fisherman when lost by reason of war activity was also provided for by order in council; that the matter of protecting the implements of his trade-his boat and his gear-was under consideration, and that it was the intention of the government to provide some compensation to those who would lose through war activities the implements of their calling. The principle was to provide for replacement at government expense of whatever implements of trade might be destroyed, in order to keep these people in production without any delay, because most of the fishermen who carry on this occupation as a method of earning their livelihood would be too poor to replace their implements if these were lost in large quantities. On that basis it was thought in the public interest to give assurance to the fishermen that they would be taken care of; that their implements would be replaced if they were lost; that that would encourage them to stay in the industry, which, we were told, some were threatening to abandon because of the great risks to which they were exposed.
At the time this matter came up, the whole of the regulations of the scheme had not been embodied in any legislation or order in council but was being elaborated by the officials of the Department of Fisheries. Since then we have been able to bring into concrete form what we thought would be fair provision to compensate those who might suffer losses of their fishing gear. This is the reason why this

was presented in the form of an order in council under the War Measures Act, as a sequence of other measures taken for the protection of the persons and personal belongings of fishermen.
As to why the administration of the pro-* visions of this order in council is left to the* Minister of Fisheries, I see no special reason, except that apparently the governor in council had enough confidence in the minister of the department to leave this function in his hands.

The whole principle of dealing with public money on this basis is wrong. It should be done under a statute, and it should not be left to the discretion of the minister no matter how fair-minded he may be. The principle is wrong: it is wrong in the fisheries department, in the agriculture department, in every department of government. You are dealing here with taxpayers' money. I wonder what the people of this country, who are now being called upon to pay more and more and more in the way of direct taxation, will think when they find out that 25 per cent of all the taxes they pay for the purposes of the war effort is being diverted to other objects. That is the indictment against the budget: 25 per cent of the money which the people are to contribute is being frittered away on useless agencies which are costing huge sums of money and are in no way connected directly with the war.
It will be argued, of course, that this arises out of the war. In a measure that is true, but I think there are many instances where large amounts of public money, contributed by people who are already being taxed up to the limit, will be paid out under the authority of orders in council for purposes not directly connected with the war. The people of Canada are willing to give to the war, but they are not willing to give carte blanche to this government or any minister of this government to switch war taxation to purposes which are not directly connected with the war.
I object to the principle of this order in council. I object to the power being left to the minister. With respect to the order in council passed under the War Measures Act, compensating for life or property damage of fishermen or others, that ought to be included in a statute of this parliament. The principle of legislation by order in council has gone absolutely beyond all limitation in this country.
Our control over government expenditures is gone. I wonder if the public realize that. I cannot emphasize it too much. I am not saying it especially in connection with this bill, but we see the principle illustrated every day-violation of the right of parliament to deal with public expenditure in matters that are really not war expenditures at all. I protest against that principle and against the operations under it. It is a wrong principle, and the operations are wrong. Parliament should not give its imprimatur to this class of legislation. The leader of the opposition talks about the powers of the minister with regard to this legislation. I have always been taught that an order in council had the same effect as a statute, that the minister is governed by the provisions of an order in council just as he is governed by the provisions of a statute. That being so, all he can do is act as trustee and administer the order in council according to its provisions. I do not think the fishermen of Nova Scotia or of Canada generally would expect anybody to do better in this regard than the head of this department, who has special knowledge of and is especially concerned with the problems of the fishermen.

To an extent this is extra legislation for the benefit of the fishermen, but only to an extent. Let us look at the practical end of it and see how it works out. The shore fisherman lives in remote fishing districts, on the headlands. As a rule he has a humble house. His house and furniture are not worth a great deal of money. In my county the houses of the shore fishermen are clean and sanitary, but not expensive. The hazard to the fisherman's property so far as a war damage insurance scheme is concerned is not as great as in the towns where buildings are closer together and extensive damage can be done. So that there are two reasons why the fisherman's situation is different: his property is not worth as much as property in the town, and the hazard is smaller because his dwelling is in a remote place.

There have been submarines off the Pacific coast, and the fishermen know it. They are greatly alarmed about the presence of these submarines, because they realize that if they' are out on the fishing banks and a submarine shows up it is not only the boat that is in danger, but their very lives, because a submarine might endeavour to sink the boat and drown the men so that no information will get back which will disclose its whereabouts. The fishermen have that in mind, and it is a serious thought. We are endeavouring to catch all the fish we possibly can in order to feed the people of Great Britain, and yet the fishermen are told that if they insure their boats to the full extent they will not be covered by this $2,000 compensation which the government has brought down by order in council.

Homes remain stationary; if an aeroplane passes over and drops a bomb, a house may be demolished. That is true, but on the other hand the fisherman goes right into the danger, and that makes all the difference. I believe there would be greater satisfaction all round if the government would amend the order in council and put the fishermen on the same status as owners of houses that are insured. I do not think it is asking too much. The government could do this up to $3,000, and if a fisherman had a boat worth $6,000 he could go to an insurance company and insure for the other $3,000. May I tell the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg why that subsidy was given. At the outbreak of the war the naval department -was short of ships, and a number of large new fishing vessels had just been completed. The naval department took them over without permission. They just notified the owners that they were taking over the new boats, some of which were splendid, new vessels costing as much as 845,000. I am speaking of the fall of 1939. Some of these vessels had only recently been launched. In my opinion it was a mistake to follow that policy. The government should not have bought these boats outright. The naval department should have leased them and had naval boats built; and, when their own boats were built, they could then have returned the other boats back instead of retaining fish boats in the naval service. These fish boats are not adapted to the protection of our coasts. They are good enough for surveys and for scouting, but it is not possible to place anti-aircraft guns on such vessels because it would shake them to pieces. The reason why the 8150 subsidy was given is that, since 1939, prices have increased, and to enable the cannery men to order new fish boats adequate for their work an inducement was held out whereby the government undertook to pay the difference in price as between 1939 and 1942. There is nothing unfair about it, and I hope that we shall hear no more complaints from the mari-times about what British Columbia is getting. If ever that argument starts we shall have a free-for-all, and we can tell plenty about what the maritimes have received.
The minister, I submit, should reconsider the order in council. We are not asking too much when we plead on behalf of the great class of fishermen who own boats worth from $2,000 up, that the same provision be made for them as has been made for those people who own homes. These fishermen cannot obtain insurance. The statement was made by the Minister of Finance that they could, but they come back with a different statement, indicating that they are unable to procure insurance. In the light of all the facts; in view of the great danger that exists on the

The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare says that he thinks that $2,000 is fair, for the reasons I have just given. Let me quote what he said. But here first, is an article in a paper giving a list of Japanese boats they are trying to sell in British Columbia, those that are left, the poorer and cheaper ones. Here are some of the values:
Glendale V	 $14,500
May 8	 8,750
Springtime V	  12,400
That gives you some idea of the value of the boats that we must have. Here is what the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare said, as reported on page 3927 of Hansard:
I hope we do not get to the radical point

the "gimme's" such as we see from western Canada. That is apparently what this is developing into-"give us this," "give us that." I am willing to back them up in what is reasonable, but we cannot adopt a policy of digging into the treasury to support this and that and extend this and that luxury to this and the other.
Let me give you a picture of the "luxury" the hon. gentleman refers to, and I know of what I speak. The best fishing for these fishermen is for about an hour at dusk and an hour at dawn. They may fish in between, but those are the best hours. In order to get to the grounds at dawn they must leave at about two o'clock in the morning. At this time of the year dawn is about three o'clock and it takes about three hours to get to the fishing grounds, which are about thirty miles offshore. So that they must leave shortly

War Risk Insurance
after midnight. They fish on the way out for what they can get, then they fish for an hour or so at dawn. They then hang around all day, since it would not pay them to come back and go out again in the evening. They may fish through the day and get a few, but they generally try to snatch a few hours' sleep. They are out in the open Pacific where there is no barrier between them and Japan. They fish in what is known as the graveyard of the Pacific, where they are subject to the full swell of the Pacific ocean. You can imagine the comfortable sleep a man will get under conditions like that. At dusk he goes fishing again, and then he starts for home, getting in about ten or eleven o'clock. He may have a good catch, or he may have only three fish. I have seen a man come in with only three fish worth 45 cents apiece. He must sell his catch. He has to wait his turn. There may be 150 men waiting at the buyer's float. Then he has to go to another place to get his gas, and to another place to get his food. Then it is time for him to start out on his next morning's work. This is the day after day life of the fisherman which is described by the hon. member behind me as a life of luxury. If I could tell him what the western fishermen think of the life of a lawyer, and particularly a Nova Scotia lawyer, it would do him good, or at least would be illuminating. These fishermen take all the risks of the sea and of poor catches. However smart a fisherman may be, he is not responsible for the whims of a school of fish, which may happen to run 100 miles further out or fifty or thirty miles away. It may be that he has no luck at all, but fishes all season and does not catch enough fish to pay for his gas and oil, let alone the upkeep of his boat. On top of all that, he now has this further hazard of being bombed. The lighthouse that was bombed by the Japanese was in my district, right in the centre of the fishing industry.
I wish to quote from a letter I received the other day from the Kyuquot Trailers Cooperative association, one of the finest instances of cooperation I have ever heard of. Twenty years ago they were poor, dissatisfied, hard-luck people, barely able to make a living. Then they got together and said: "We will cooperate." Without any government assistance at all, they put in their nickels and dimes and dollars and established their cooperative organization, and now they have a fine business community. They run their own packer, and so on. This man writes on behalf of the whole association, and incidentally I might say to the Minister of Finance that this man would like to see insurance covering fish packers and seiners as well as trolling boats. This is the letter he writes to a member of the ministry:
As you may not be aware, the fishermen joined together in this association produced 3,500,000 pounds of salmon during the season of 1941; and that, owing to the removal of the Japanese fishermen from the west coast, the white fishermen now alone must brave the dangers of the sea, and in addition, be subject to surprise attacks by any lurking submarine, which may do great damage, and when fishing offshore, might prevent these small boats from reaching shore.
As all the salmon suitable for canning has been earmarked for British consumption, and the fishermen have been urged to go out and produce as much as possible, irrespective of the dangers to which they expose themselves, we were quite surprised to learn from the new proposed bill for "war risk insurance" submitted in the House of Commons that salt water fishermen had been excluded, while the inland fishermen, who might be considered almost out of danger, could have their boats and equipment covered.
We wish to point out that most of the fishermen have invested their all in their boats and equipment, and they are not alone risking their property, but also their lives in trying to produce the foodstuff which is so urgently required; also, we might say that they expose themselves to the same dangers as the naval forces, who at least will be looked after, and their dependents compensated in case of loss of life.
He goes on to speak of submarines being off the coast and says that the white fishermen have made a very successful attempt to replace the Japanese fishermen and that their output is on the increase. Then he says, and this bears out what the hon. member for New Westminster said:
As far as is known to the writer there is no "war risk insurance" available to this type of boat, varying in value from $2,000 to $6,000, and if it could be procured the premiums would likely be so high that the fishermen could not afford it.
If you could assure these fishermen that they would receive the same consideration as the other classes of Canadian citizens as regards property, although it may be classed as floating, we feel sure you will have rendered the producers of an essential foodstuff a great service and the returns from that source would justify your support for an all-out effort in production.
You should not forget that these small boats help to protect our west coast by assisting the naval and air forces with any information they may gather without any military standing.
Here is another letter, only a short one:
What in the world is the matter with the government, when they are prepared to insure boats on lakes and fresh water rivers but not those who go to sea?
Take the case of us fellows at Kyuquot, we are fishing daily, anywhere from three to twenty miles offshore in the open Pacific. If there is
War Risk Insurance

any commercial activity going on anywhere, that is exposed to as much potential war risk, I'd like to hear of it.
I value my boat at $5,000. It represents ten years of struggle and savings. I can't afford to carry even the ordinary insurance for fire and wreck for this district.
Ask the Minister of Finance to get out an atlas of Vancouver island, then run his finger along the -west coast till he comes to the promontory of Cape Cook, then ask him how' he'd feel, fishing offshore from there twenty miles, in a 36-foot troller.
Fishermen generally, accept as their lot the ordinary hazards of this business, but feel they should be covered by damage from enemy action.
That is a genuine man. I can certify that he is a first-class fisherman and a fine type of man.
The minister says tha-t he is introducing this change by order in council. I do not go to the extent the leader of the opposition did in suggesting all the dreadful things the minister might do under the order in council. I think the order in council will be administered fairly. There is no reason why it should not be, but I regret that this scheme was brought into effect by order in council, instead of by legislation which we could have discussed. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, if you wanted to be mean-of course, you would not be-you could rule that it was out of order to discuss the order in council because it is not before the house. It is the bill that is before the house. Why was not this order in council or its contents put before the fisheries committee? Why has not the fisheries committee had a meeting for years and years? If we had had this order in council before the fisheries committee it would have been put into better shape, but it was not sent to that committee at all. It was sent to the banking and commerce committee composed mostly of financial men who would not know a fisherman from a haystack if they met one. A lot of time would have been saved if the order in council had been put before the fisheries committee; both the ministers would have then been better informed, and they would have had a better order in council to put before the house.
We asked that the order in council be read into Hansard, but even that was not done. We were told that, instead, the order in council would be put on Votes and Proceedings. But we cannot get Votes and .Proceedings in any quantity -without paying ten cents apiece for them, ten cents for a little bit of paper. The price is prohibitive if one wants to send tw'o or three hundred to the fishermen. I was able to get only a dozen. The order in council should at least have been put on Hansard, and should have been sent to the fisheries committee, where we could have discussed it.

I object very strongly to this compensation being called "compassionate relief". Where is the compassion? Where is the relief? Is it not a just and a right thing? Are you telling these fishermen that they are being treated compassionately? I object to the suggestion that it is a hand-out. It is not like the $160,000 down in Nova Scotia, two dollars and a half to this boat and eight and a half to that boat, engaged in deep-sea fishing. I would call that political relief, and it has been going on for a long time. If a soldier or a sailor or an airman is killed, we do not call the care that we take of his widow and orphans compassionate relief.
There is another objection to the order in council. It will not allow the fishermen to insure beyond the $2,000 that will be granted by the government. They allow a man to insure his house beyond that. The house owner can insure his house up to $50,000 if he likes, and why in all fairness should we not allow the fisherman to do the same? But if the fisherman insures beyond this amount of $2,000, he loses the compensation granted by the government. The fishermen cannot get commercial insurance anyhow.
Under the bill the government are going to have a scheme of insurance of their own on buildings. It is to be done through an insurance agent, but the government pays the money. If you can insure a house through the government, why not a fisherman's boat? The Minister of Finance says that marine insurance is a new form of insurance to him, with which he is not familiar and that he does not care to go into marine insurance. The marine insurance people will take care of that. All we ask the Minister of Finance to do is to foot the bill, and in the last resort it always comes to the government.
An hon. member sitting behind me has pointed out the objection to having only one boat- insured. As I said the other day, a cannery must have a number of boats or it could not.keep the cannery running; and if a fisherman cannot afford more than one boat the cannery will lease him one. The fisherman and the cannery man must be able if they need, to have more than one boat. He told us clearly and distinctly that there would be only one boat and only two men on a boat. And now the order in council-

I have been trying to get myself in a position to give a satisfactory answer to inquiries such as this for two or three months. I have been trying to get this bill through, and I thought I might shorten the discussion by sending the bill to the banking and commerce committee and having them discuss it there, but it has come back to the house and, as hon. gentlemen know, a considerable amount of discussion has taken place. We have passed only one section; we are now on section 2, and I want to get back to section 2 as soon as possible. But this debate on the protection of fishermen came up. As I said the other day I felt that we would have to meet the situation in some way, in order to clear the way and get ahead with the bill, though I hoped the discussion on that point would not last too long. Probably it was not strictly in order, though ships are referred to in this section. However, I could not really raise a point of order, because in any event IMr. Cruickshank.]
the discussion probably would run outside the bill, and I had no objection to hon. members discussing this fisheries order in council.
I received the wire which the hon. gentleman has read, or one like it, and I replied to it at once, stating that I could not authorize the insurance companies to accept applications or to write insurance policies now, because I did not have any legislation. I want to remind the house that I had power, or the government had power to enact legislation by order in council. That was express power under legislation, not under the War Measure Act but under the War Appropriation Act. Section 2 of every war appropriation act from 1915 up to the present time has contained this as one of the powers- granted to the government:
(c) promoting the continuance of trade, industry and business communications, whether by means of insurance or indemnity against war risk or in any other manner whatsoever

I hope I am not making a statement that is at all shocking to the democratic sensibilities of hon. members of this house, but if I had the matter to do over again, contrary to what was said this afternoon by the leader of the opposition, I would have drawn up an order in council. Then I would have had a system of war risk insurance in operation, and I would not be embarrassed by telegrams such as the one just read by the hon. member. We have done things almost as important, or more important, by order in council, but we decided to bring this to the House of Commons. I still have the floor, Mr. Chairman. That was just by way of answer to the hon. member for Fraser Valley. The hon. member for St. Paul's asked what the rate of insurance is on our coasts; that is, war risk insurance, not marine insurance. I obtained the information by telephoning to Montreal this morning. The rate of insurance on the Pacific is II per cent for three months,

War Risk Insurance
provided the vessel does not go west of cape Spencer, which I understand is on Skagway. I think only the large boats engaged in halibut fishing go that far, and if the smaller vessels wanted coverage the rate might be less. I have no information which confirms the statement made this afternoon that insurance is not procurable. My information is that war risk insurance is procurable at these rates, which are substantial rates but not beyond reason. If for instance a company or a fisherman or anyone else had a boat worth $3,000 which he wished to insure against war risk at this rate, it would amount to 5 per cent for the whole year.
That is $150 of an operating charge which he would have in this time of war, more than in time of peace. It is $150, but it is a business expense which is assumed by all kinds of owners of fishing craft. On the Atlantic coast the rate is 2 per cent for three months and, as the member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley) said, they put it on. They insure their schooners there. What is being asked of the government this afternoon is in effect that we should cut down all these policies by $3,000, and pay the premium for these fishing companies on the first $3,000 or the last $3,000, because the moment we say that we will assume the first $3,000 free, then every policy of $20,000 comes down to $17,000, because they get the premium paid by the government instead of paying it themselves. They are not asking for that, and I do not want to do that.
The comparison has been made between fishing boats and houses. There is no comparison. The fisherman gets the same protection as everyone else gets on his house, the same protection as everyone else gets on his furniture. Further than that, he gets free compensation for certain effects if they are lost at sea, and he gets insurance against personal damage or death, the same as members of the forces under the Pension Act. Now we come along and are taking a piece of business property, a piece of his capital, and are giving him free compensation for that, in addition, up to $2,000. I do not think we should be asked to go further.
If marine rates go out of all reason and there is a need to be met there, then the government may be compelled to adopt and put into effect a government marine insurance scheme. But I certainly will not, if I can avoid it, incorporate that in this bill because it is a different class of risk, a different kind of business. I would have to have a different set of advisers, people who know marine insurance, rather than fire insurance, because this is comparable to fire insurance. Marine insurance is the sort of insurance we are dealing with here.
I suggest that hon. gentlemen accept what has been done and allow the government to get ahead with this important bill. The leader of the opposition asked why we did not put this provision in this measure. I made it clear that it does not belong in this bill. It is entirely foreign to the bill, and that is the pressure which I have been obliged to resist from the beginning, to incorporate into this measure provision for property which does not belong with the property covered under the bill, as to which the risk is different, the business is different, and so forth. It would ruin our whole scheme if we did that.
The hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross) said what was true when he stated that we are throwing away $200,000 or $300,000 of easy premiums by cutting out ships on the great lakes. Why am I cutting out ships on the great lakes? I am doing so in order to avoid the charge of discrimination. Would there be a charge of discrimination? Certainly there would be. There are such charges in two of the letters which were read to-day by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). The charge is that we are discriminating in favour of big companies against small people. There are $200,000 or $300,000 of premiums which, it is said, we might as well have as not, but we are eliminating the ships on the great lakes so as to avoid charges of discrimination. I cannot stand here and have it said that I am sacrificing the people on the coast in favour of big interests in Ontario and Quebec.
The hon. gentleman dug out something from the order in council to indicate that a firm can get free compensation for more than one boat while the poor fisherman cannot. If I have my way, that will come out to-morrow, so that the firm will get compensation only for one boat. That is what I will do, because I will not have charges made of discrimination in favour of the big people as against the small men, or in favour of inland as against coastal interests. I cannot do it. The government has to be careful about these things.

One thing I resent, and I resent it also on the part of the Minister of Finance, is the suggestion that any private member is tying up this legislation. Certainly, if there is any tying up it is not by the members from British Columbia. We are elected to protect the interests of our constituencies, our province and the dominion as a whole, and I repeat, if there is any tying up we are not doing it. I am not quarrelling with the order in council. This is one of the few times when, in my opinion, action can be taken only by order in council. Obviously, as the minister himself said, conditions may change. The amount might change to-morrow as war conditions became either more serious or less so, either on the Pacific coast or elsewhere. But if the government can do that, there is no tying up on the part of private members. The tying up is being done by the government itself if it cannot put into effect the request of the Vancouver board of trade, that the insurance companies be instructed immediately to accept, on behalf of the government, applications for war risk insurance, all applications to be accompanied by a cheque representing the amount of deposit. Surely the government cannot say there is any tying up. That can be covered when the time comes. In the meantime, the government or its advisers-so far as this bill is concerned- apparently do not realize or have never heard of Egypt, and they have certainly never heard of the Japs. The danger is imminent and we must have action now. I do not wish to interfere with the hon. member for Fraser Valley getting a reply. I have read what he said about this bill and I have respect for his views. I wish, however, to continue my protest of three weeks ago against the policy of this bill and the change in the definition by order in council, the change in the whole bill, from the first clause to the end. In the first place, by this order in council the government is changing every definition in the Interpretation Act. You have to read the order in council into the last clause of the bill, which is the most important one of all, and the regulations are set out in nearly two pages of the bill. Is this parliament going to act as a sort of agent, a sort of life-saver for the insurance companies of the country, at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer? The only insurance we have in Canada to-day in connection with war damages of all kinds for fishermen was restricted by the committee, in the bill, first, to inland waters and extended subsequently. This bill should have been extended in the first place to coastal waters and to fishing boats and appliances which are near the danger zone on the Pacific and the Atlantic. Are we now going to relieve these insurance companies? I attended one of the meetings of the committee, and I am surprised at the action of the minister. The minister has a likable personality, but he is always very clever at special pleading for what I call certain sections of the country. He is not slow to plead the case of his own section of the country in regard to apples, potatoes,

War Risk Insurance
codfish and everything else. But when it comes to the central provinces, who are paying such a large part of the taxes, they get little or nothing. I do not represent any insurance company or loan company. I suggest that if the minister had kept the loan companies' agents out of the committee, it would have been better for everyone concerned. This country cannot stand the expense which has been imposed by the minister, assisted by his controllers and bureaucrats. These things are done by means of orders in council passed by these bureaucrats over the head of parliament.
I have no objection to war risk insurance in certain cases. These insurance companies came to parliament and asked that all kinds of risks be covered which were never contemplated either during the great war or this war. They said they were prepared to cover these risks and private bills were introduced into parliament. I opposed three or four of them which originated in Toronto. This is simply a utopian scheme which will never be carried out. We do not know just what is the real situation on the Atlantic and the Pacific. I made an appeal to the minister. Dwellings are to be covered up to a value of $3,000, but I do not know of any industrial worker who has a dwelling worth that much. We all know the deplorable state of our finances to-day.
This order in council changes many of the definitions in the interpretation section of Bill No. 56. We have the diminution value covered, applicants and so on. Where is the minister going to get this insurance? Some of these large insurance companies have made fortunes out of the premiums paid in, and they are doing very little to help the war. They do buy victory loans with trust funds, with the people's money and not their own. By this bill and the order in council the minister proposes to give these insurance companies the power to act as agents in this particular class of insurance. Power is being delegated to them to collect premiums and there will be no check on them. These companies will be a law unto themselves.
When this bill was before the house previously I objected to the second reading. At that time I said that there were two classes in the country which were not being covered, and apparently they have no special pleaders in this house. I refer to the industrial workers and the soldiers. The industrial workers used to have some property, but if we have many more of these budgets and controllers they will have property no longer. If the minister wants to do something he
should inaugurate a system of national insurance. That would do far more to cover risks on the homes of industrial workers than this bill. The rates now charged are 5, 6i and 7 per cent; the minister should take advantage of the power he has under the War Measures Act and cut this rate to 4J per cent. When it was proposed that an order in council should be passed under the War Measures Act in order to check insurance rates and mortgage rates and to institute a system of national control of mortgages, the answer was, "oh, no." These companies have made fortunes out of the poor people, and parliament should give the poor people some protection.
I know of men who have gone to the war leaving everything they had. Their property should have been covered by an order in council passed under the War Measures Act. They are more capable than three-quarters of the men in the minister's department; they gave up jobs that were just as good.
In conclusion, I say that this bill and the order in council are class legislation of the worst kind. They do not provide protection for the property of the people I have mentioned. In my opinion the government has adopted a wrong principle. I am a warm supporter of protection for the fishermen because I know of their sufferings. I have been to both coasts, and I know how they suffered during the depression. The best that this parliament can do for them is not good enough.
There should, -however, be some protection for the other two classes I have mentioned. With the present budget the fisherman or the soldier or the industrial worker will not have any property. With these budgets and controllers any property owned by the small retailer or the small wholesaler will be eliminated.	_
So what is the use of talking about a risk up to $3,000 on a dwelling, or on a fisherman's property? Under the definition as amended, what is the use of owning anything? The right to possess private property is derived from nature, not from man, and he and all his regiment of officials cannot take away that right. It existed before he was born, when the people of England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales came out here as pioneers and settled this country. But to-day all incentive to thrift has been abolished in this country. This bill and the order in council help only 50 per cent of our population, and the other 50 per cent are left to shift for themselves. Here we are reversing the policy of Macdonald, Laurier and Cartier and all those other great statesmen. I should like to see everybody own some property, whether it be some small
War Risk Insurance

business, a retail store, a mill, farm machinery, or even a cow. It is the private ownership of property that has helped to build up this country, and now we are seeing private property abolished.
I can tell the insurance companies that they had better look at the handwriting on the wall. Some of these insurance companies invested in common stocks and lost millions of dollars of the premiums that had been paid in for life insurance, and the result was that some of these companies were allowed to come to parliament and get a certificate, to which they were not entitled, to allow them to carry on.
I have every sympathy for the fisherman but I do not believe the fisherman will ever get a cent under this bill. I do not think anybody will get a cent under this bill. It is a technical bill designed by the dreamers and Utopians of all kinds who have been trying to meddle with private business in this country, with wholesalers and with retailers and the ordinary business man. The bill will never attain the objects for which it was designed.
Why is not something done about a national scheme of insurance for the soldiers? If you say anything about the soldiers, you are told: The soldier owns no property. But I know soldiers who have given up all their property, who have lost everything, even life itself, and nothing is done to insure them; but dreamers in the insurance department can present a bill like this to parliament. If this is the way we are going to do our business, it is no wonder that parliament is fast losing its influence and the respect of the taxpayers of this country. Here we are, after talking for several months, and we have not yet considered one dollar of the minister's estimates.
There is no protection provided for the industrial worker. He has lost his property already through taxation.
I suggest that this bill be left over until next year, and let us close up parliament and get home as rapidly as possible. If the minister persists in going on with bills like this we shall be here until next October. Some of these bills will have to be dropped if the louse is to close within a reasonable time.

speechtext:
Before the section carries, there is another whole aspect of it which I think should have some attention from the committee, and I fear that we shall not have time this afternoon to give it that attention.
I should like to say in a general way that I have been impressed by the work of the committee this afternoon. Those people who
are running about the country talking about the deficiencies of parliament, its carelessness and so forth, would, I think, have been enlightened had they been here to-day and observed the solicitude with which the various hon. members were looking after the interests of their constituents. After all, that is what we are here for-to look after our constituencies, which comprise Canada. I think the minister has honestly attempted to be fair to all concerned. I think he has listened with due sympathy to the requests of the various hon. members.
The matter I wish to discuss is the meaning of "value" in this bill. I note that paragraph (m) of section 2 was deleted. I was a member of the banking and commerce committee which deleted that clause, but I was never satisfied as to the reason why it was deleted. It is, I think, an important matter. The paragraph served as a sort of criterion by reference to which the minister's agents might hope to determine the extent of damage which had been done to a given piece of property-the value of the property. I wonder what, in the minister's mind, compensates in the bill for the loss which it has sustained by the deletion of that paragraph from the section. What is there in the bill now to enable those who will administer it to determine the value of a given piece of property which has been damaged?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: I was informed that the section, perhaps, did not quite represent the result of the court decisions as to what is the value under an insurance policy, and I understood that the members of the banking and commerce committee felt that the definition should be eliminated, that there should be no definition of value, and that value should be settled now as it is under a fire insurance policy, in accordance with legal principles. I understand it is very difficult to define. I know that Mr. Leonard thought he had defined it about in accordance with the results of the decisions, but some members of the committee disagreed with him, and it was decided to cut it out.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: It will leave the legal remedy. I think that is fair.
